title: Response to application from respondent Florida

pages.text:
Capital Case No. 26A524
IN THE
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
WILLIAM REAVES
Petitioner,
v.
STATE OF FLORIDA,
Respondent.
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE FLORIDA SUPREME COURT
RESPONSE TO APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR OCTOBER 20, 2026, AT 6:00 P.M.
William Reaves, a Florida prisoner under an active death warrant with an 
execution scheduled for October 20, 2026, asks this Court to stay his execution for the 
first-degree murder of Indian River County Sherrif Deputy Richard Raczkoski on 
September 23, 1986, for which Reaves confessed, while it considers whether to grant 
certiorari. However, the questions Reaves presents (clemency and mitigation review)
do not warrant a stay under Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. 880, 895 (1983). As 
thoroughly explained in the accompanying Brief in Opposition to certiorari, Reaves’s 
questions do not merit this Court’s review. Therefore, this Court should deny the stay.
As an initial point, Reaves also asks for a stay based on a request he made to 
intervene in Guardado v. Richard Comerford, Sec’y, Dep’t of Corr., et. al., No. 3:26-

2
cv-02596-MMH-SJH (M.D. Fla. Sept. 28, 2026) where Guardado filed a 42 U.S.C. § 
1983 action challenging Florida’s administration of the lethal injection protocol.
Reaves raised an Eighth Amendment as-applied challenge to Florida’s protocol in 
state court but did not raise that claim here. Further, he offers no argument under 
the Barefoot v. Estelle standard related to the lethal injection claim. Those failings 
are fatal to his request for a stay. Clearly, Reaves cannot meet the standard for a 
stay. There is no basis to stay this certiorari review on the speculation that Reaves 
will be permitted to intervene, obtain a stay in United States District Court for the 
Middle District of Florida, and have a significant likelihood of success on the merits. 
This is especially true where Reaves did not raise a similar attack in state court on 
the ground Guardado raised in federal court and Reaves did not file his own § 1983 
action before his warrant was signed or shortly thereafter. Instead, he waited until 
four days before his execution to move to intervene in another capital defendant’s 
federal action. This Court should find Reaves’s attempt to intervene in Guardado’s 
federal case irrelevant to the stay requested in the instant certiorari petition. 
A stay of execution is not granted as a “matter of course.” It is an equitable 
remedy, and “equity must remain sensitive to the State’s strong interest in enforcing 
its criminal judgments without undue interference from the federal courts.” Hill v. 
McDonough, 547 U.S. 573, 583–84 (2006). To obtain a stay, Reaves must establish a 
reasonable probability that four Justices would vote to grant certiorari, a significant 
possibility of reversal, and a likelihood of irreparable harm. Barefoot, 463 U.S. at 895. 
This Court has further emphasized that last-minute litigation and dilatory claims

3
weigh heavily against equitable relief. Gomez v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for N. Dist. of Cal., 503 
U.S. 653, 654 (1992). Reaves cannot satisfy these requirements.
Reaves’s first question is addressed to the constitutional sufficiency of his 
clemency process. The Florida Supreme Court noted that its precedent acknowledges 
Justice O’Connor’s concurrence in Ohio Adult Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 272, 
276 (1998) and emphasized the “unlimited discretion vested solely in the executive 
branch” regarding clemency. It applied its precedent holding that a capital defendant 
does not have a right to clemency records nor does he have a constitutional right to 
effective clemency counsel. Finaly, the court found Reaves’s claim that his hearing 
loss “may have caused him to miss critical information during the clemency process” 
too speculative to support relief. Reaves, 2026 WL 3071534 at *3. Reaves’s second 
question asks whether the Florida Supreme Court conducted a proper analysis of his 
mitigation presentation in his 2002 postconviction ineffective assistance of counsel 
claim, in his 2012 successive postconviction litigation, and as part of a procedurally 
barred cumulative error/manifest injustice claim in his state habeas petition under 
active warrant. Reaves v. State, No. SC2026-1512, 2026 WL 3071534 (Fla. Oct. 14, 
2026). Neither question warrants certiorari review, much less, satisfies the high 
standard for granting a stay of an execution for a forty-year-old murder of a Deputy 
Sheriff. Reaves has not shown that Florida’s clemency procedures warrant review in 
light of his speculative claim or that the application of a state procedural bar conflicts 
with a decision of this Court, a federal circuit court, or another state supreme court. 
There is no basis necessitating this Court’s review.

4
Stays of Execution
There is a “strong equitable presumption against the grant of a stay where a 
claim could have been brought at such a time as to allow consideration of the merits 
without requiring entry of a stay.” Nelson v. Campbell, 541 U.S. 637, 650 (2004). 
Equity must also consider “an inmate’s attempt at manipulation.” Gomez v. U.S. Dist. 
Ct. for N. Dist. of Cal., 503 U.S. 653, 654 (1992). Equity does not reward last-minute 
litigation designed to delay the imposition of lawful sentences. See Nelson, 541 U.S. 
at 650 (holding that there is a “strong equitable presumption against the granting of 
a stay where a claim could have been brought at such a time as to allow consideration 
of the merits without requiring entry of a stay”). The dilatory posture of Reaves’s
claim weighs heavily against a stay.
“Both the State and the victims of crime have an important interest in the 
timely enforcement of a sentence.” Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998). 
This Court has highlighted the State’s and the victims’ interests in the timely 
enforcement of the death sentence. Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149-51 (2019). 
The people of Florida, as well as surviving victims and their families, “deserve better” 
than the “excessive” delays that now typically occur in capital cases. Id. at 149. This 
Court has stated that courts should “police carefully” against last minute claims being 
used “as tools to interpose unjustified delay” in executions. Id. at 150. Also, this Court 
has stated that last-minute stays of execution should be the “extreme exception, not 
the norm.” Id.

5
To be granted a stay of execution, Reaves must establish three factors: (1) a 
reasonable probability that the Court would vote to grant certiorari; (2) a significant 
possibility of reversal if review were granted; and (3) a likelihood of irreparable injury 
to the applicant in the absence of a stay. Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. at 895. Reaves
must establish all three factors, however, he has not.
Probability of This Court Granting Certiorari
As to the first factor, there is little chance that four justices of this Court would 
vote to grant certiorari review on the issues raised here. Reaves has cited no conflict 
or unsettled question of law for this Court’s review.
This Court has stated that “pardon and commutation decisions have not 
traditionally been the business of courts; as such, they are rarely, if ever, appropriate 
subjects for judicial review.” Ohio Adult Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 272, 276 
(1998) (quoting Conn. Bd. of Pardons v. Dumschat, 452 U.S. 458, 464 (1985)). Even if 
“some minimal procedural safeguards apply to clemency proceedings,” Woodard, 523 
U.S. at 289 (O’Connor, J., concurring) (original emphasis), they were satisfied when 
Reaves was appointed clemency counsel, submitted an application and information 
for clemency, and was granted an interview. The Constitution does not require the 
States to enact a specific clemency mechanism. Herrera v. Collins, 506 U.S. 390, 414 
(1993). Further, Reaves’s latest attempt to relitigate the Florida Supreme Court’s 
review of its 2002 and 20121 mitigation presentation rests on the independent and 
1 In Reaves’s second successive postconviction litigation, he challenged the mitigation 
review under Porter v. McCollum, 558 U.S. 30 (2009). Reaves v. State, 91 So. 3d 782 
(Fla. 2012) (finding Porter is no retroactive to cases on collateral review). See

6
adequate ground of a state law procedural bar. This Court has long recognized state 
law bars as a valid basis to deny certiorari review. Here, Reaves fails the first Barefoot 
v. Estelle factor, which alone is sufficient to deny the motion for a stay.
Even without reliance on this independent and adequate state ground to deny 
certiorari, the granting of certiorari is unlikely because the Florida Supreme Court 
found that Reaves’s constitutional challenge was meritless based on its multiple 
decisions rejecting similar challenges to the clemency process. See Lukehart v. State, 
No. SC2026-0736, 2026 WL 1480328, at *5 n. 13 (Fla. May 27, 2026) (reiterating that 
“under Florida and federal law, a defendant has no constitutional right to effective 
collateral counsel”), cert. denied, 146 S. Ct. 2697 (2026); Randolph v. State, 422 So. 
3d 166, 174 (Fla.) (rejecting constitutional challenges to clemency process), cert. 
denied, 146 S. Ct. 819 (2025); Zakrzewski v. State, 415 So. 3d 203, 211 (Fla.), cert. 
denied, 146 S. Ct. 57 (2025); Marek v. State, 14 So. 3d 985, 998 (Fla.), cert. denied, 
557 U.S. 960 (2009). See also, Bowles v. DeSantis, 934 F.3d 1230, 1242 n.8 (11th Cir. 
2019) (finding because “there is no constitutional right to clemency, there is no 
constitutional right to effective assistance of counsel in clemency proceedings.”); 
Banks v. Sec'y, Fla. Dep't. of Corr., 592 F. App'x 771, 773 (11th Cir. 2014) 
(determining that clemency counsel's ineffectiveness was not a basis for challenging 
Florida's clemency process). Further, the basis for Reaves’s clemency challenge, 
namely, his hearing loss, was determined to be speculative and therefore unworthy 
generally, Reaves v. Sec’y Fla. Dep’t of Corr., 872 F.3d 1137 (11th Cir. 2017) (rejecting 
federal habeas petition raising ineffective assistance of penalty phase counsel).

7
of relief. Reaves’s challenge to his clemency process does not warrant certiorari 
consideration and shows that it is unlikely certiorari would be granted.
Likewise, both the Florida Supreme Court and the Eleventh Circuit Court of 
Appeals reviewed penalty phase counsel’s effectiveness in presenting mitigation and 
determined counsel rendered constitutionally reasonable representation under 
Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668 (1984). Reaves v. State, 826 So. 2d 932 (Fla. 
2002) Reaves, 91 So. 3d at 783; Reaves, 872 F.3d at 1151-60. Reaves’s recent attack 
on the mitigation decision was found procedurally barred. That determination does 
not require certiorari review and shows Reaves has failed the first prong of the 
Barefoot v. Estelle standard. 
Significant Possibility of Reversal
As to the second factor, there is not a significant possibility of reversal on the 
issue raised by Reaves. The repeated acknowledgement of the unlimited discretion 
vested in the Governor to decide clemency issues and the speculative nature of 
Reaves’s hearing loss to challenge the sufficiency of the process he admitted he 
received, shows the possibility of reversal is low. Similarly, the application of a state 
procedural bar to the mitigation claim shows the possibility on that factor is equally 
low as it is an independent and adequate basis for the decision below. As noted above, 
the claim was also found meritless given the multiple times the Florida Supreme 
Court reviewed Reaves’s mitigation case under Strickland. This Court does not grant 
review where the decision below rests on independent and adequate state law, one 
that would not support reversal on the merits. Likewise, review is not likely given

8
the speculative and conclusory allegations raised in state court. Thus, Reaves’s fails 
this factor as well.
Irreparable Injury
As to the third factor of irreparable injury, there is none. While the execution 
will result in Reaves’s death, that is the inherent nature of a death sentence. The 
factors for granting a stay are taken from the standard for granting a stay as applied 
to normal civil litigation, which is not a natural fit in capital cases. In the capital 
context, more should be required for irreparable injury rather than the execution 
itself. Otherwise, this factor would automatically be satisfied in every capital case. In 
other contexts, this Court has clarified that the “purpose of such a stay is to prevent 
the execution date from ‘interfer[ing] with the orderly processing of a petition on 
direct review by this Court.’” Rodriguez v. Texas, 515 U.S. 1307, 1307-08 (1995). And 
in Williams v. Missouri, 463 U.S. 1301, 1301-02 (1983), this Court explained that a 
stay would be warranted to prevent a defendant from being executed before having 
the opportunity to fully present his claim that his death sentence was 
unconstitutionally imposed. But those situations do not exist here. Likewise, this is 
not a case in which denying his stay would result in the execution of a defendant who 
should not be executed. Reaves faces no actual identifiable harm by the denial of his 
motion for stay under these circumstances. As discussed above, neither of his 
questions merit certiorari review as one is speculative at best and the other is 
procedurally barred. The denial of a stay will not hamper review of his claims.

9
Moreover, this Court has stated in the capital context that “the relative harms 
to the parties” must still be considered, including “the State’s significant interest in 
enforcing its criminal judgments.” Nelson, 541 U.S. at 649-50. Here, Reaves does not 
provide any unique or special argument as to why a last-minute stay is warranted in 
his specific case that outweighs the State’s interest in enforcing the law. Without 
finality, “the criminal law is deprived of much of its deterrent effect.” Calderon v. 
Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 555-56 (1998). The real finality is the execution. Because 
Reaves points to no specific argument in support of this factor other than the 
imposition of his lawful sentence, he fails this prong as well.
Reaves fails to meet any of the three factors for being granted a stay of 
execution. Therefore, the application for a stay of execution should be denied.
Respectfully submitted,
JAMES UTHMEIER
ATTORNEY GENERAL OF FLORIDA
